query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, substituting about 5 at% of the other refractory elements with molybdenum (Mo) will promote the formation of Mo-stabilized coherent precipitates and enhance lattice distortion, thereby improving elevated‐temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary HEA, for example, with approximately 40 at% Ti, 40 at% Ni, and the remaining 20 at% distributed among other refractory elements (e.g., Nb, Ta, etc.) that combine to form a predominantly single-phase solid solution at high temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce 5 at% Mo into the alloy composition by substituting an equivalent fraction of the other secondary refractory elements.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature conditions, e.g., tests performed in the range of 800–1200 °C under tensile and creep loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of Mo-rich, coherent precipitates within the primary solid-solution matrix together with increased lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Mo, acting as a beta stabilizer, enhances solid solution strengthening and encourages the nucleation of fine, coherent precipitates. These structural features impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding at high temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-modified alloy will show improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties, with higher yield strength and slower creep rates compared to the baseline alloy. While the estimated improvement might be on the order of approximately 10–20%, the exact magnitude is uncertain due to processing and microstructural variables.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary HEA without the Mo substitution.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected for HEAs where Ti and Ni are primary constituents (with each element in the range of 5–35 at%) and under high-temperature conditions (800–1200 °C); results may vary if the alloy deviates from these compositional or operating ranges.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of strengthening or creep resistance improvement is uncertain, as it will depend on factors such as heat treatment, exact composition, precipitate morphology, and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples using identical processing routes: one set with the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary HEA composition and one set with the modified composition incorporating 5 at% Mo (via equivalent substitution). Subject both sets to standardized heat treatments to allow microstructural equilibration. Then perform elevated-temperature tensile tests and creep experiments in the range of 800–1200 °C.
measurements: Creep rate under a fixed load
Microstructural analysis (using TEM or XRD) to detect and characterize Mo-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., <5% increase in yield strength and no observable decrease in creep rate) relative to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal Mo-induced precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites []. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,].
